stem: If a line intersects sides AB and AC of a \(\triangle\) ABC at D and E respectively and is parallel to BC, prove that \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{AC}}\) (see Fig. 6.13).
solution:
DE \(\parallel\) BC (Given)

So, \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}}\) (Theorem 6.1)

or, \(\frac{\text{DB}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{\text{EC}}{\text{AE}}\)

or, \(\frac{\text{DB}}{\text{AD}} + 1 = \frac{\text{EC}}{\text{AE}} + 1\)

or, \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{AE}}\)

So, \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{AC}}\)

stem: ABCD is a trapezium with AB \(\parallel\) DC. E and F are points on non-parallel sides AD and BC respectively such that EF is parallel to AB (see Fig. 6.14). Show that \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FC}}\).
solution:
Let us join AC to intersect EF at G (see Fig. 6.15).

AB \(\parallel\) DC and EF \(\parallel\) AB (Given)

So, EF \(\parallel\) DC (Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other)

Now, in \(\triangle\) ADC,

EG \(\parallel\) DC (As EF \(\parallel\) DC)

So, \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{AG}}{\text{GC}}\) (Theorem 6.1) ... (1)

Similarly, from \(\triangle\) CAB,

\(\frac{\text{CG}}{\text{AG}} = \frac{\text{CF}}{\text{BF}}\)

i.e., \(\frac{\text{AG}}{\text{GC}} = \frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FC}}\) ... (2)

Therefore, from (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FC}}\)

stem: In Fig. 6.16, \(\frac{\text{PS}}{\text{SQ}} = \frac{\text{PT}}{\text{TR}}\) and \(\angle\) PST = \(\angle\) PRQ. Prove that PQR is an isosceles triangle.
solution:
It is given that \(\frac{\text{PS}}{\text{SQ}} = \frac{\text{PT}}{\text{TR}}\).

So, ST \(\parallel\) QR (Theorem 6.2)

Therefore, \(\angle\) PST = \(\angle\) PQR (Corresponding angles) ... (1)

Also, it is given that \(\angle\) PST = \(\angle\) PRQ ... (2)

So, \(\angle\) PRQ = \(\angle\) PQR [From (1) and (2)]

Therefore, PQ = PR (Sides opposite the equal angles)

i.e., PQR is an isosceles triangle.

context: Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets :
stem: All circles are __________ . (congruent, similar)
solution:
**similar**.

All circles have the same shape — one is always an enlargement of another — but they need not have the same radius, so they need not be congruent.

context: Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets :
stem: All squares are __________ . (similar, congruent)
solution:
**similar**.

Every square has all angles \(90^\circ\) and all sides equal, so any two squares have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Their sides need not be equal, so they need not be congruent.

context: Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets :
stem: All __________ triangles are similar. (isosceles, equilateral)
solution:
**equilateral**.

Every equilateral triangle has all three angles \(60^\circ\), so any two of them are similar by AAA. Two isosceles triangles need not be similar — their apex angles can differ.

context: Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets :
stem: Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (a) their corresponding angles are __________ and (b) their corresponding sides are __________ . (equal, proportional)
solution:
(a) **equal**  (b) **proportional**.

Both conditions are needed. Fig. 6.7 shows a square and a rhombus of equal sides — proportional sides but unequal angles — and they are not similar.

context: Give two different examples of pair of
stem: similar figures.
solution:
Two examples:

1. Any two circles (of different radii).
2. Any two squares (of different sides).

Other acceptable pairs: two equilateral triangles, two regular hexagons, a photograph and its enlargement.

context: Give two different examples of pair of
stem: non-similar figures.
solution:
Two examples:

1. A square and a rhombus that is not a square — corresponding sides can be proportional, but the angles are not equal.
2. A rectangle and a square — the angles are all \(90^\circ\), but the sides are not proportional.

Other acceptable pairs: a circle and an ellipse, a scalene triangle and an equilateral triangle.

stem: State whether the following quadrilaterals are similar or not:
solution:
**Not similar.**

In Fig. 6.8 the quadrilateral PQRS has all four sides 1.5 cm and ABCD has all four sides 3 cm, so the corresponding sides ARE proportional, in the ratio \(\frac{1.5}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\).

But ABCD is a square, so each of its angles is \(90^\circ\), while PQRS is a rhombus whose angles are not \(90^\circ\). The corresponding angles are therefore not equal.

Similarity needs BOTH conditions, so the two quadrilaterals are not similar.

context: In Fig. 6.17, (i) and (ii), DE \(\parallel\) BC. Find EC in (i) and AD in (ii).
stem: Find EC in (i).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC, DE \(\parallel\) BC, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem

\(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}}\)

From the figure AD = 1.5 cm, DB = 3 cm and AE = 1 cm.

\(\frac{1.5}{3} = \frac{1}{\text{EC}}\)

\(\text{EC} = \frac{3 \times 1}{1.5} = 2\)

So EC = 2 cm.

context: In Fig. 6.17, (i) and (ii), DE \(\parallel\) BC. Find EC in (i) and AD in (ii).
stem: Find AD in (ii).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC, DE \(\parallel\) BC, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem

\(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}}\)

From the figure DB = 7.2 cm, AE = 1.8 cm and EC = 5.4 cm.

\(\frac{\text{AD}}{7.2} = \frac{1.8}{5.4} = \frac{1}{3}\)

\(\text{AD} = \frac{7.2}{3} = 2.4\)

So AD = 2.4 cm.

context: E and F are points on the sides PQ and PR respectively of a \(\triangle\) PQR. For each of the following cases, state whether EF \(\parallel\) QR :
stem: PE = 3.9 cm, EQ = 3 cm, PF = 3.6 cm and FR = 2.4 cm
solution:
EF \(\parallel\) QR if and only if \(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{EQ}} = \frac{\text{PF}}{\text{FR}}\) (converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem).

\(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{EQ}} = \frac{3.9}{3} = 1.3\)

\(\frac{\text{PF}}{\text{FR}} = \frac{3.6}{2.4} = 1.5\)

The ratios are not equal, so **EF is not parallel to QR**.

context: E and F are points on the sides PQ and PR respectively of a \(\triangle\) PQR. For each of the following cases, state whether EF \(\parallel\) QR :
stem: PE = 4 cm, QE = 4.5 cm, PF = 8 cm and RF = 9 cm
solution:
\(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{QE}} = \frac{4}{4.5} = \frac{8}{9}\)

\(\frac{\text{PF}}{\text{RF}} = \frac{8}{9}\)

The ratios are equal, so by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem **EF \(\parallel\) QR**.

context: E and F are points on the sides PQ and PR respectively of a \(\triangle\) PQR. For each of the following cases, state whether EF \(\parallel\) QR :
stem: PQ = 1.28 cm, PR = 2.56 cm, PE = 0.18 cm and PF = 0.36 cm
solution:
Here the WHOLE sides are given, so first find the remaining parts:

\(\text{EQ} = \text{PQ} - \text{PE} = 1.28 - 0.18 = 1.10\) cm

\(\text{FR} = \text{PR} - \text{PF} = 2.56 - 0.36 = 2.20\) cm

Now

\(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{EQ}} = \frac{0.18}{1.10} = \frac{9}{55}\)

\(\frac{\text{PF}}{\text{FR}} = \frac{0.36}{2.20} = \frac{9}{55}\)

The ratios are equal, so **EF \(\parallel\) QR**.

stem: In Fig. 6.18, if LM \(\parallel\) CB and LN \(\parallel\) CD, prove that \(\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AN}}{\text{AD}}\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC, LM \(\parallel\) CB.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{MB}} = \frac{\text{AL}}{\text{LC}}\).

Adding 1 to both sides, \(\frac{\text{AM} + \text{MB}}{\text{MB}} = \frac{\text{AL} + \text{LC}}{\text{LC}}\), i.e. \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{MB}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{LC}}\).

So \(\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AL}}{\text{AC}}\) ... (1)

Similarly, in \(\triangle\) ACD, LN \(\parallel\) CD gives

\(\frac{\text{AN}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{\text{AL}}{\text{AC}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AN}}{\text{AD}}\).

stem: In Fig. 6.19, DE \(\parallel\) AC and DF \(\parallel\) AE. Prove that \(\frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FE}} = \frac{\text{BE}}{\text{EC}}\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC, DE \(\parallel\) AC.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{BD}}{\text{DA}} = \frac{\text{BE}}{\text{EC}}\) ... (1)

In \(\triangle\) ABE, DF \(\parallel\) AE.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{BD}}{\text{DA}} = \frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FE}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{BF}}{\text{FE}} = \frac{\text{BE}}{\text{EC}}\).

stem: In Fig. 6.20, DE \(\parallel\) OQ and DF \(\parallel\) OR. Show that EF \(\parallel\) QR.
solution:
In \(\triangle\) PQO, DE \(\parallel\) OQ.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{EQ}} = \frac{\text{PD}}{\text{DO}}\) ... (1)

In \(\triangle\) PRO, DF \(\parallel\) OR.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{PF}}{\text{FR}} = \frac{\text{PD}}{\text{DO}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{PE}}{\text{EQ}} = \frac{\text{PF}}{\text{FR}}\).

So, in \(\triangle\) PQR, EF divides PQ and PR in the same ratio, and by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem EF \(\parallel\) QR.

stem: In Fig. 6.21, A, B and C are points on OP, OQ and OR respectively such that AB \(\parallel\) PQ and AC \(\parallel\) PR. Show that BC \(\parallel\) QR.
solution:
In \(\triangle\) OPQ, AB \(\parallel\) PQ.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{OA}}{\text{AP}} = \frac{\text{OB}}{\text{BQ}}\) ... (1)

In \(\triangle\) OPR, AC \(\parallel\) PR.

By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(\frac{\text{OA}}{\text{AP}} = \frac{\text{OC}}{\text{CR}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{OB}}{\text{BQ}} = \frac{\text{OC}}{\text{CR}}\).

So, in \(\triangle\) OQR, BC divides OQ and OR in the same ratio, and by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem BC \(\parallel\) QR.

stem: Using Theorem 6.1, prove that a line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle parallel to another side bisects the third side. (Recall that you have proved it in Class IX).
solution:
Let \(\triangle\) ABC have D as the mid-point of AB, and let the line through D parallel to BC meet AC at E. We must show AE = EC.

Since DE \(\parallel\) BC, Theorem 6.1 gives

\(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}}\)

D is the mid-point of AB, so AD = DB, i.e. \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = 1\).

Therefore \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}} = 1\), so AE = EC.

Hence E is the mid-point of AC — the line bisects the third side.

stem: Using Theorem 6.2, prove that the line joining the mid-points of any two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side. (Recall that you have done it in Class IX).
solution:
Let \(\triangle\) ABC have D and E as the mid-points of AB and AC respectively. We must show DE \(\parallel\) BC.

Since D is the mid-point of AB, AD = DB, so \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = 1\).

Since E is the mid-point of AC, AE = EC, so \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}} = 1\).

Therefore \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{DB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{EC}}\).

DE divides the two sides AB and AC in the same ratio, so by Theorem 6.2 DE \(\parallel\) BC.

stem: ABCD is a trapezium in which AB \(\parallel\) DC and its diagonals intersect each other at the point O. Show that \(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{BO}} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{DO}}\).
solution:
Through O, draw a line EO parallel to DC, meeting AD at E and BC at F. (This is the construction the textbook's hint gives.)

Since AB \(\parallel\) DC and EF \(\parallel\) DC, we also have EF \(\parallel\) AB.

In \(\triangle\) ADC, EO \(\parallel\) DC, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem

\(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{AO}}{\text{OC}}\) ... (1)

In \(\triangle\) ABD, EO \(\parallel\) AB, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem

\(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{BO}}{\text{OD}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{OC}} = \frac{\text{BO}}{\text{OD}}\).

Rearranging, \(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{BO}} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{DO}}\).

stem: The diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD intersect each other at the point O such that \(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{BO}} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{DO}}\). Show that ABCD is a trapezium.
solution:
This is the converse of the previous question.

We are given \(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{BO}} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{DO}}\), which rearranges to

\(\frac{\text{AO}}{\text{OC}} = \frac{\text{BO}}{\text{OD}}\) ... (1)

Through O draw EO \(\parallel\) DC, meeting AD at E.

In \(\triangle\) ADC, EO \(\parallel\) DC, so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem

\(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{AO}}{\text{OC}}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\frac{\text{AE}}{\text{ED}} = \frac{\text{BO}}{\text{OD}}\).

So in \(\triangle\) ABD, the line EO divides AD and BD in the same ratio, and by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem EO \(\parallel\) AB.

But EO \(\parallel\) DC by construction, so AB \(\parallel\) DC.

A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides parallel is a trapezium, so ABCD is a trapezium.

stem: In Fig. 6.29, if PQ \(\parallel\) RS, prove that \(\triangle\) POQ ~ \(\triangle\) SOR.
solution:
PQ \(\parallel\) RS (Given)

So, \(\angle\) P = \(\angle\) S (Alternate angles)

and \(\angle\) Q = \(\angle\) R

Also, \(\angle\) POQ = \(\angle\) SOR (Vertically opposite angles)

Therefore, \(\triangle\) POQ ~ \(\triangle\) SOR (AAA similarity criterion)

stem: Observe Fig. 6.30 and then find \(\angle\) P.
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) PQR,

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{RQ}} = \frac{3.8}{7.6} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QP}} = \frac{6}{12} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{2}\)

That is, \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{RQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QP}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PR}}\)

So, \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) RQP (SSS similarity)

Therefore, \(\angle\) C = \(\angle\) P (Corresponding angles of similar triangles)

But \(\angle\) C = \(180^\circ - \angle\) A \(- \angle\) B (Angle sum property)

\(= 180^\circ - 80^\circ - 60^\circ = 40^\circ\)

So, \(\angle\) P = \(40^\circ\)

stem: In Fig. 6.31, OA . OB = OC . OD. Show that \(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) C and \(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) D.
solution:
OA . OB = OC . OD (Given)

So, \(\frac{\text{OA}}{\text{OC}} = \frac{\text{OD}}{\text{OB}}\) ... (1)

Also, we have \(\angle\) AOD = \(\angle\) COB (Vertically opposite angles) ... (2)

Therefore, from (1) and (2), \(\triangle\) AOD ~ \(\triangle\) COB (SAS similarity criterion)

So, \(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) C and \(\angle\) D = \(\angle\) B (Corresponding angles of similar triangles)

stem: A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. If the lamp is 3.6 m above the ground, find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.
solution:
Let AB denote the lamp-post and CD the girl after walking for 4 seconds away from the lamp-post (see Fig. 6.32).

From the figure, DE is the shadow of the girl. Let DE be \(x\) metres.

Now, BD = 1.2 m \(\times\) 4 = 4.8 m.

Note that in \(\triangle\) ABE and \(\triangle\) CDE,

\(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) D (Each is of \(90^\circ\) because lamp-post as well as the girl are standing vertical to the ground)

and \(\angle\) E = \(\angle\) E (Same angle)

So, \(\triangle\) ABE ~ \(\triangle\) CDE (AA similarity criterion)

Therefore, \(\frac{\text{BE}}{\text{DE}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{CD}}\)

i.e., \(\frac{4.8 + x}{x} = \frac{3.6}{0.9}\)   (90 cm = \(\frac{90}{100}\) m = 0.9 m)

i.e., \(4.8 + x = 4x\)

i.e., \(3x = 4.8\)

i.e., \(x = 1.6\)

So, the shadow of the girl after walking for 4 seconds is 1.6 m long.

stem:
In Fig. 6.33, CM and RN are respectively the medians of \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) PQR. If \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR, prove that :

(i) \(\triangle\) AMC ~ \(\triangle\) PNR

(ii) \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}}\)

(iii) \(\triangle\) CMB ~ \(\triangle\) RNQ
solution:
(i) \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR (Given)

So, \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{RP}}\) ... (1)

and \(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) P, \(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) Q and \(\angle\) C = \(\angle\) R ... (2)

But AB = 2 AM and PQ = 2 PN (As CM and RN are medians)

So, from (1), \(\frac{2\,\text{AM}}{2\,\text{PN}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{RP}}\)

i.e., \(\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{PN}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{RP}}\) ... (3)

Also, \(\angle\) MAC = \(\angle\) NPR [From (2)] ... (4)

So, from (3) and (4), \(\triangle\) AMC ~ \(\triangle\) PNR (SAS similarity) ... (5)

(ii) From (5), \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{RP}}\) ... (6)

But \(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{RP}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}}\) [From (1)] ... (7)

Therefore, \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}}\) [From (6) and (7)] ... (8)

(iii) Again, \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\) [From (1)]

Therefore, \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\) [From (8)] ... (9)

Also, \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{2\,\text{BM}}{2\,\text{QN}}\)

i.e., \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{BM}}{\text{QN}}\) ... (10)

i.e., \(\frac{\text{CM}}{\text{RN}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{BM}}{\text{QN}}\) [From (9) and (10)]

Therefore, \(\triangle\) CMB ~ \(\triangle\) RNQ (SSS similarity)

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (i)
solution:
**Yes.**

In \(\triangle\) ABC: \(\angle\) A = \(60^\circ\), \(\angle\) B = \(80^\circ\), \(\angle\) C = \(40^\circ\).

In \(\triangle\) PQR: \(\angle\) P = \(60^\circ\), \(\angle\) Q = \(80^\circ\), \(\angle\) R = \(40^\circ\).

All three pairs of corresponding angles are equal.

Criterion: **AAA**. \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR.

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (ii)
solution:
**Yes.**

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{RP}} = \frac{2.5}{5} = \frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\)

All three pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

Criterion: **SSS**. \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) QRP.

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (iii)
solution:
**No — the triangles are not similar.**

The sides of the first triangle are 2, 2.7 and 3; those of the second are 4, 5 and 6.

Taking them in increasing order, \(\frac{2}{4} = 0.5\), \(\frac{2.7}{5} = 0.54\), \(\frac{3}{6} = 0.5\).

The three ratios are not all equal, so no correspondence makes the sides proportional and no similarity criterion applies.

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (iv)
solution:
**Yes.**

\(\frac{\text{MN}}{\text{QP}} = \frac{2.5}{5} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{\text{NL}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}\)

The angle between those two sides is the same in both: \(\angle\) M = \(\angle\) Q = \(70^\circ\).

Two pairs of sides are proportional and the INCLUDED angles are equal.

Criterion: **SAS**. \(\triangle\) MNL ~ \(\triangle\) QPR.

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (v)
solution:
**No — the triangles are not similar.**

Two sides are given in each triangle and one angle, but the angle is NOT the included angle in both.

In \(\triangle\) ABC the given angle is \(\angle\) A = \(80^\circ\), which lies between AB and AC — and AC is not given.

In \(\triangle\) DEF the given angle is \(\angle\) F = \(80^\circ\), which lies between DF and EF.

SAS needs the angle to be the one BETWEEN the two proportional sides in both triangles, so the criterion does not apply here.

context: State which pairs of triangles in Fig. 6.34 are similar. Write the similarity criterion used by you for answering the question and also write the pairs of similar triangles in the symbolic form :
stem: Pair (vi)
solution:
**Yes.**

In \(\triangle\) DEF: \(\angle\) D = \(70^\circ\), \(\angle\) E = \(80^\circ\), so \(\angle\) F = \(180^\circ - 70^\circ - 80^\circ = 30^\circ\).

In \(\triangle\) PQR: \(\angle\) P = \(80^\circ\), \(\angle\) R = \(30^\circ\), so \(\angle\) Q = \(180^\circ - 80^\circ - 30^\circ = 70^\circ\).

So \(\angle\) D = \(\angle\) Q, \(\angle\) E = \(\angle\) P and \(\angle\) F = \(\angle\) R.

Criterion: **AA**. \(\triangle\) DEF ~ \(\triangle\) PQR.

stem: In Fig. 6.35, \(\triangle\) ODC ~ \(\triangle\) OBA, \(\angle\) BOC = \(125^\circ\) and \(\angle\) CDO = \(70^\circ\). Find \(\angle\) DOC, \(\angle\) DCO and \(\angle\) OAB.
solution:
DOB is a straight line, so \(\angle\) DOC and \(\angle\) BOC form a linear pair.

\(\angle\) DOC = \(180^\circ - \angle\) BOC = \(180^\circ - 125^\circ = 55^\circ\)

In \(\triangle\) DOC, by the angle sum property,

\(\angle\) DCO = \(180^\circ - \angle\) CDO \(- \angle\) DOC = \(180^\circ - 70^\circ - 55^\circ = 55^\circ\)

Since \(\triangle\) ODC ~ \(\triangle\) OBA, corresponding angles are equal, so

\(\angle\) OAB = \(\angle\) OCD = \(55^\circ\)

So \(\angle\) DOC = \(55^\circ\), \(\angle\) DCO = \(55^\circ\) and \(\angle\) OAB = \(55^\circ\).

stem: Diagonals AC and BD of a trapezium ABCD with AB \(\parallel\) DC intersect each other at the point O. Using a similarity criterion for two triangles, show that \(\frac{\text{OA}}{\text{OC}} = \frac{\text{OB}}{\text{OD}}\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) AOB and \(\triangle\) COD,

AB \(\parallel\) DC and AC is a transversal, so \(\angle\) BAO = \(\angle\) DCO (Alternate angles)

AB \(\parallel\) DC and BD is a transversal, so \(\angle\) ABO = \(\angle\) CDO (Alternate angles)

Therefore \(\triangle\) AOB ~ \(\triangle\) COD (AA similarity criterion)

Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional, so

\(\frac{\text{OA}}{\text{OC}} = \frac{\text{OB}}{\text{OD}}\)

stem: In Fig. 6.36, \(\frac{\text{QR}}{\text{QS}} = \frac{\text{QT}}{\text{PR}}\) and \(\angle\) 1 = \(\angle\) 2. Show that \(\triangle\) PQS ~ \(\triangle\) TQR.
solution:
\(\angle\) 1 = \(\angle\) 2, i.e. \(\angle\) PQR = \(\angle\) PRQ.

Sides opposite equal angles are equal, so PQ = PR ... (1)

We are given \(\frac{\text{QR}}{\text{QS}} = \frac{\text{QT}}{\text{PR}}\).

Using (1) to replace PR by PQ,

\(\frac{\text{QR}}{\text{QS}} = \frac{\text{QT}}{\text{PQ}}\), i.e. \(\frac{\text{QT}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{PQ}}{\text{QS}}\) ... (2)

Now in \(\triangle\) PQS and \(\triangle\) TQR,

\(\frac{\text{PQ}}{\text{QS}} = \frac{\text{QT}}{\text{QR}}\) [From (2)]

and \(\angle\) PQS = \(\angle\) TQR (Same angle, \(\angle\) Q)

Therefore \(\triangle\) PQS ~ \(\triangle\) TQR (SAS similarity criterion)

stem: S and T are points on sides PR and QR of \(\triangle\) PQR such that \(\angle\) P = \(\angle\) RTS. Show that \(\triangle\) RPQ ~ \(\triangle\) RTS.
solution:
In \(\triangle\) RPQ and \(\triangle\) RTS,

\(\angle\) RPQ = \(\angle\) RTS (Given, since \(\angle\) P = \(\angle\) RTS)

\(\angle\) PRQ = \(\angle\) TRS (Same angle, \(\angle\) R)

Two pairs of corresponding angles are equal.

Therefore \(\triangle\) RPQ ~ \(\triangle\) RTS (AA similarity criterion)

stem: In Fig. 6.37, if \(\triangle\) ABE \(\cong\) \(\triangle\) ACD, show that \(\triangle\) ADE ~ \(\triangle\) ABC.
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABE \(\cong\) \(\triangle\) ACD (Given)

Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, so

AB = AC and AE = AD ... (1)

Therefore \(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{AC}}\) ... (2)

(Since AD = AE and AB = AC, both ratios equal the same number.)

Now in \(\triangle\) ADE and \(\triangle\) ABC,

\(\frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{AC}}\) [From (2)]

and \(\angle\) DAE = \(\angle\) BAC (Same angle, \(\angle\) A)

Therefore \(\triangle\) ADE ~ \(\triangle\) ABC (SAS similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.38, altitudes AD and CE of \(\triangle\) ABC intersect each other at the point P. Show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) AEP ~ \(\triangle\) CDP
solution:
In \(\triangle\) AEP and \(\triangle\) CDP,

\(\angle\) AEP = \(\angle\) CDP = \(90^\circ\) (CE \(\perp\) AB and AD \(\perp\) BC)

\(\angle\) APE = \(\angle\) CPD (Vertically opposite angles)

Therefore \(\triangle\) AEP ~ \(\triangle\) CDP (AA similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.38, altitudes AD and CE of \(\triangle\) ABC intersect each other at the point P. Show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) CBE
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABD and \(\triangle\) CBE,

\(\angle\) ADB = \(\angle\) CEB = \(90^\circ\) (AD \(\perp\) BC and CE \(\perp\) AB)

\(\angle\) ABD = \(\angle\) CBE (Same angle, \(\angle\) B)

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) CBE (AA similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.38, altitudes AD and CE of \(\triangle\) ABC intersect each other at the point P. Show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) AEP ~ \(\triangle\) ADB
solution:
In \(\triangle\) AEP and \(\triangle\) ADB,

\(\angle\) AEP = \(\angle\) ADB = \(90^\circ\) (CE \(\perp\) AB and AD \(\perp\) BC)

\(\angle\) EAP = \(\angle\) DAB (Same angle, \(\angle\) A)

Therefore \(\triangle\) AEP ~ \(\triangle\) ADB (AA similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.38, altitudes AD and CE of \(\triangle\) ABC intersect each other at the point P. Show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) PDC ~ \(\triangle\) BEC
solution:
In \(\triangle\) PDC and \(\triangle\) BEC,

\(\angle\) PDC = \(\angle\) BEC = \(90^\circ\) (AD \(\perp\) BC and CE \(\perp\) AB)

\(\angle\) PCD = \(\angle\) BCE (Same angle, \(\angle\) C)

Therefore \(\triangle\) PDC ~ \(\triangle\) BEC (AA similarity criterion)

stem: E is a point on the side AD produced of a parallelogram ABCD and BE intersects CD at F. Show that \(\triangle\) ABE ~ \(\triangle\) CFB.
solution:
ABCD is a parallelogram, so AB \(\parallel\) DC and AD \(\parallel\) BC.

In \(\triangle\) ABE and \(\triangle\) CFB,

\(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) C (Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal)

AD \(\parallel\) BC, i.e. AE \(\parallel\) BC, with BE as transversal, so

\(\angle\) AEB = \(\angle\) CBF (Alternate angles)

Two pairs of corresponding angles are equal.

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABE ~ \(\triangle\) CFB (AA similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.39, ABC and AMP are two right triangles, right angled at B and M respectively. Prove that:
stem: \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) AMP
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) AMP,

\(\angle\) ABC = \(\angle\) AMP = \(90^\circ\) (Given — right angled at B and at M)

\(\angle\) BAC = \(\angle\) MAP (Same angle, \(\angle\) A)

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) AMP (AA similarity criterion)

context: In Fig. 6.39, ABC and AMP are two right triangles, right angled at B and M respectively. Prove that:
stem: \(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PA}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{MP}}\)
solution:
From part (i), \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) AMP.

Corresponding sides of similar triangles are in the same ratio, so

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AM}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{MP}} = \frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PA}}\)

Taking the last two of these,

\(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{PA}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{MP}}\)

context: CD and GH are respectively the bisectors of \(\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) EGF such that D and H lie on sides AB and FE of \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) EFG respectively. If \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG, show that:
stem: \(\frac{\text{CD}}{\text{GH}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{FG}}\)
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG (Given)

So \(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) F and \(\angle\) ACB = \(\angle\) FGE ... (1)

CD bisects \(\angle\) ACB and GH bisects \(\angle\) EGF, so

\(\angle\) ACD = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) FGH = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\angle\) FGE

From (1), \(\angle\) ACD = \(\angle\) FGH ... (2)

Now in \(\triangle\) ACD and \(\triangle\) FGH,

\(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) F [From (1)]

\(\angle\) ACD = \(\angle\) FGH [From (2)]

Therefore \(\triangle\) ACD ~ \(\triangle\) FGH (AA similarity criterion)

Corresponding sides are proportional, so \(\frac{\text{CD}}{\text{GH}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{FG}}\).

context: CD and GH are respectively the bisectors of \(\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) EGF such that D and H lie on sides AB and FE of \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) EFG respectively. If \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG, show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) DCB ~ \(\triangle\) HGE
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG (Given), so \(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) E and \(\angle\) ACB = \(\angle\) FGE.

CD and GH are the bisectors of \(\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) FGE, so halving both sides of the second equality,

\(\angle\) DCB = \(\angle\) HGE

Now in \(\triangle\) DCB and \(\triangle\) HGE,

\(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) E

\(\angle\) DCB = \(\angle\) HGE

Therefore \(\triangle\) DCB ~ \(\triangle\) HGE (AA similarity criterion)

context: CD and GH are respectively the bisectors of \(\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) EGF such that D and H lie on sides AB and FE of \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) EFG respectively. If \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG, show that:
stem: \(\triangle\) DCA ~ \(\triangle\) HGF
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) FEG (Given), so \(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) F and \(\angle\) ACB = \(\angle\) FGE.

CD and GH are the bisectors of \(\angle\) ACB and \(\angle\) FGE, so halving both sides of the second equality,

\(\angle\) DCA = \(\angle\) HGF

Now in \(\triangle\) DCA and \(\triangle\) HGF,

\(\angle\) A = \(\angle\) F

\(\angle\) DCA = \(\angle\) HGF

Therefore \(\triangle\) DCA ~ \(\triangle\) HGF (AA similarity criterion)

stem: In Fig. 6.40, E is a point on side CB produced of an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC. If AD \(\perp\) BC and EF \(\perp\) AC, prove that \(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) ECF.
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABC is isosceles with AB = AC, so the angles opposite those sides are equal:

\(\angle\) ABC = \(\angle\) ACB ... (1)

Note that \(\angle\) ECF is the same angle as \(\angle\) ACB, since E lies on CB produced.

Now in \(\triangle\) ABD and \(\triangle\) ECF,

\(\angle\) ADB = \(\angle\) EFC = \(90^\circ\) (AD \(\perp\) BC and EF \(\perp\) AC)

\(\angle\) ABD = \(\angle\) ECF [From (1)]

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) ECF (AA similarity criterion)

stem: Sides AB and BC and median AD of a triangle ABC are respectively proportional to sides PQ and QR and median PM of \(\triangle\) PQR (see Fig. 6.41). Show that \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR.
solution:
We are given \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{PM}}\) ... (1)

AD is the median to BC, so BD = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)BC; PM is the median to QR, so QM = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)QR.

Therefore \(\frac{\text{BD}}{\text{QM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\text{BC}}{\frac{1}{2}\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\)

So from (1), \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{QM}} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{PM}}\)

Now in \(\triangle\) ABD and \(\triangle\) PQM all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional, so

\(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) PQM (SSS similarity criterion)

Hence \(\angle\) ABD = \(\angle\) PQM, i.e. \(\angle\) ABC = \(\angle\) PQR ... (2)

Finally, in \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) PQR,

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\) [From (1)]

\(\angle\) ABC = \(\angle\) PQR [From (2)] — and this is the INCLUDED angle between those two sides

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR (SAS similarity criterion)

stem: D is a point on the side BC of a triangle ABC such that \(\angle\) ADC = \(\angle\) BAC. Show that \(\text{CA}^2 = \text{CB} \cdot \text{CD}\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\) ADC and \(\triangle\) BAC,

\(\angle\) ADC = \(\angle\) BAC (Given)

\(\angle\) ACD = \(\angle\) BCA (Same angle, \(\angle\) C)

Therefore \(\triangle\) ADC ~ \(\triangle\) BAC (AA similarity criterion)

Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional, so

\(\frac{\text{CA}}{\text{CB}} = \frac{\text{CD}}{\text{CA}}\)

Cross-multiplying, \(\text{CA}^2 = \text{CB} \cdot \text{CD}\).

stem: Sides AB and AC and median AD of a triangle ABC are respectively proportional to sides PQ and PR and median PM of another triangle PQR. Show that \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR.
solution:
We are given \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{PM}}\) ... (1)

The textbook's hint gives the construction: produce AD to E such that AD = DE, and produce PM to N such that PM = MN. Join EC and NR.

In \(\triangle\) ABD and \(\triangle\) ECD, BD = DC (AD is a median), AD = DE (construction) and \(\angle\) ADB = \(\angle\) EDC (vertically opposite), so the triangles are congruent (SAS). Hence AB = EC.

Similarly PQ = NR.

Also AE = 2 AD and PN = 2 PM.

Substituting into (1),

\(\frac{\text{EC}}{\text{NR}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{2\,\text{AD}}{2\,\text{PM}} = \frac{\text{AE}}{\text{PN}}\)

So in \(\triangle\) AEC and \(\triangle\) PNR all three pairs of sides are proportional, giving

\(\triangle\) AEC ~ \(\triangle\) PNR (SSS similarity criterion)

Therefore \(\angle\) DAC = \(\angle\) MPR.

By the same argument applied on the other side, \(\angle\) BAD = \(\angle\) QPM.

Adding, \(\angle\) BAC = \(\angle\) QPR ... (2)

Finally, in \(\triangle\) ABC and \(\triangle\) PQR,

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}}\) [From (1)]

\(\angle\) BAC = \(\angle\) QPR [From (2)] — the included angle

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR (SAS similarity criterion)

stem: A vertical pole of length 6 m casts a shadow 4 m long on the ground and at the same time a tower casts a shadow 28 m long. Find the height of the tower.
solution:
The pole and the tower are both vertical, and the sun's rays fall at the same angle at the same time, so the two triangles formed (object, its shadow, the ray) are similar by the AA criterion.

Let the height of the tower be \(h\) metres.

\(\frac{\text{height of pole}}{\text{shadow of pole}} = \frac{\text{height of tower}}{\text{shadow of tower}}\)

\(\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{28}\)

\(h = \frac{6 \times 28}{4} = 42\)

So the height of the tower is 42 m.

stem: If AD and PM are medians of triangles ABC and PQR, respectively where \(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR, prove that \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{PM}}\).
solution:
\(\triangle\) ABC ~ \(\triangle\) PQR (Given)

So \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\) ... (1)

and \(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) Q ... (2)

AD is the median to BC, so BD = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)BC; PM is the median to QR, so QM = \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)QR.

Therefore \(\frac{\text{BD}}{\text{QM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\text{BC}}{\frac{1}{2}\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}}\) [Using (1)] ... (3)

Now in \(\triangle\) ABD and \(\triangle\) PQM,

\(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{QM}}\) [From (3)]

\(\angle\) B = \(\angle\) Q [From (2)] — the included angle

Therefore \(\triangle\) ABD ~ \(\triangle\) PQM (SAS similarity criterion)

Corresponding sides are proportional, so \(\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{PM}}\).
